summary: Explains how the Path Computation Element architecture can serve Abstraction and Control of Traffic-Engineered Networks, a framework for orchestrating virtual networks across large multi-domain networks. It describes how PCE components and the PCE Communication Protocol fit the roles ACTN needs for computing paths.

plainLanguage.summary: A big trip across many countries needs a travel planner who knows the maps. This shows how a path-planning helper can work with a system that controls many networks at once.

subtitle: How path computation elements support abstraction and control of traffic-engineered networks

tldr.problem: Modern networks span multiple domains and require orchestration platforms to abstract underlying complexity and control large-scale virtual networks, but existing path computation techniques were designed for single-domain scenarios.
tldr.mechanism: The Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture provides hierarchical coordination, abstraction mechanisms, and policy translation capabilities that align with the ACTN framework's three-tier controller model.
tldr.outcome: PCE and its protocol (PCEP) can serve as the foundation for ACTN implementations, enabling multi-domain path computation, network abstraction, and service provisioning across complex networks.

today: RFC 8637 is an Informational specification examining how PCE applies to ACTN. ACTN itself remains an active area of IETF work. PCE, PCEP, and Hierarchical PCE are used in real network deployments, and operators use these mechanisms for multi-domain coordination and virtual network orchestration.

sections.title: Path Computation and Network Control
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) is a component that computes network paths based on a graph of available resources and a set of constraints (like bandwidth, latency, or cost). It responds to requests from Path Computation Clients (PCCs) via the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP).

A stateful PCE goes further: it tracks not just the network topology but also active services and reserved resources, allowing it to compute paths while considering how new paths will interact with existing ones. An active PCE can even modify or reroute existing paths on behalf of clients.

Abstraction and Control of TE Networks (ACTN) is a framework for orchestrating virtual networks across large multi-domain networks. It defines a three-tier hierarchy: a Customer Network Controller (CNC) representing customer needs at the top, a Multidomain Service Coordinator (MDSC) coordinating across multiple domains in the middle, and Provisioning Network Controllers (PNCs) managing individual domains at the bottom. The MDSC abstracts underlying network complexity for customers while managing interactions between domains.
sections.plainLanguage: A path planner (PCE) remembers which roads are busy. A big trip coordinator (MDSC) knows about all the local guides (PNCs) and makes sure trips across countries work smoothly while hiding details from customers.

sections.title: Hierarchical Coordination and Abstraction
sections.content:
ACTN's three-tier hierarchy maps naturally to PCE's hierarchical model. In Hierarchical PCE (H-PCE), a Parent PCE coordinates path computation across multiple domains by requesting constrained path segments from Child PCEs responsible for individual domains. The Parent PCE can stitch these segments together into end-to-end paths, and it maintains an abstracted view of the topology that hides domain-internal details while exposing domain interconnections.

In ACTN terms, the MDSC acts like a Parent PCE and each PNC acts like a Child PCE. The MDSC computes end-to-end virtual network paths using abstracted topology information from PNCs, which in turn compute domain-specific path segments. This allows the MDSC to present customers with a simplified network view while leveraging PCE's sophisticated multi-domain path computation capabilities.

Abstraction is critical in multi-domain networks. The MDSC cannot expose every link and node in every domain to customers, as that would overwhelm them with details they don't control. Instead, it builds an abstracted topology showing only the connectivity that customers can use. PCE can construct this abstraction using BGP-LS advertisements from Child PCEs or by exchanging link-state information via PCEP itself using the PCEP-LS mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: A parent trip planner doesn't tell customers about every road; they show the main highways and airport connections. They work with local guides who know the detailed maps, get path plans from them, and stitch them into a full itinerary.

sections.title: Key ACTN Functions Realized by PCE
sections.content:
Multidomain coordination is where the MDSC must coordinate path computation across multiple independent domains. Hierarchical PCE with stateful support handles this: the Parent PCE receives a request for an end-to-end path, queries Child PCEs for feasible segments, and stitches them together, accounting for inter-domain constraints and resource interactions.

Customer mapping translates customer virtual network requests into domain-specific provisioning commands. The PCE-initiated LSP model (RFC 8281) enables the MDSC (acting as a Parent PCE) to send path setup messages (PCInitiate) to PNCs (Child PCEs), which then provision the paths in their domains. The MDSC can apply business logic and policy to map abstract customer requests into concrete network operations.

Service coordination groups multiple LSPs belonging to the same customer virtual network and optimizes them together. PCEP extensions can associate LSPs with a VN construct, allowing PCEs to apply optimization techniques across all paths in a VN slice, rather than optimizing each path independently.

Abstraction** is handled through topology exchange: PNCs advertise abstracted topology to the MDSC via BGP-LS or PCEP-LS, limiting visible details to what the MDSC needs for path computation and what customers might need to understand service availability.
sections.plainLanguage: The coordinator (MDSC) asks each local guide (PNC) for available routes, plans an end-to-end trip, sends orders to each guide to set up their segment, groups all a customer's trips so they work well together, and shows the customer only the summary map they need.

sections.title: ACTN Interfaces and PCEP
sections.content:
ACTN defines two key interfaces. The CNC-MDSC Interface (CMI) connects customer applications to the MDSC, allowing customers to request virtual networks and services. The MDSC-PNC Interface (MPI) connects the MDSC to individual PNCs, allowing the MDSC to request path computation and LSP provisioning from each domain.

PCEP is well-suited to both interfaces. PCEP's request/reply model allows the CNC to be a path computation client and the MDSC to be a server; the MDSC can be a client to PNCs for its own path computation requests. PCEP's stateful extensions (storing active LSP state) and PCE-initiated LSP capabilities fit the MDSC's need to control and track virtual network services. PCEP's hierarchical design scales naturally to multi-domain environments, and the protocol's extensibility allows encoding of policy and service-related information.

The recursive nature of PCEP supports cascading MDSCs: if a top-level MDSC delegates part of the network to lower-level MDSCs, each can use PCEP to coordinate with the next level, maintaining the same protocol from customer interface to domain network control.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers talk to the coordinator (MDSC) using the standard protocol; the coordinator talks to local guides (PNCs) using the same protocol. If there are multiple levels of coordinators, they all use the same language, so messages scale up and down the hierarchy.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Operators have flexibility in choosing how to realize ACTN functions. While this specification shows how PCE and PCEP can serve all roles, operators might use PCEP for multidomain coordination via Hierarchical PCE but use NETCONF, RESTCONF, or BGP-LS for topology abstraction or customer mapping. The specification documents the options and shows which PCEP extensions are needed for each.

Key PCEP extensions supporting ACTN include stateful PCE (RFC 8231) for tracking LSP state across the MDSC and PNCs, PCE-initiated LSP setup (RFC 8281) for the MDSC to provision paths on demand, hierarchical PCE (RFC 6805) for multi-domain coordination, and emerging extensions for VN association, policy attachment, and link-state distribution.

The specification identifies gaps in PCEP at the time of publication that would benefit from future extensions, such as standardized mechanisms for expressing complex policy and abstraction levels.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators can build a coordination system using PCE and PCEP for path planning, or mix in other tools for managing topology details or customer requests. The specification shows all the pieces and how they fit together.
